title: The Invention of the Artificial Heart
summary: How Robert Jarvik designed the Jarvik-7, the first artificial heart successfully implanted in a human patient by surgeon William DeVries in 1982, giving seriously ill patients more time to live.
poll: The artificial heart is one of the most important inventions ever created for giving seriously ill patients hope and more time to live.

versions.title: A Pump for the Heart
versions.text:
See that small pump. It is a new heart. It helps blood move.

Some hearts get too sick. A sick heart cannot pump well. A new heart can help.

Long ago, doctors had no good plan. A sick heart just got worse. There was no real fix.

In 1982, a man made a new heart. His name was Jarvik. It was made of strong parts. It was not a real heart from a body.

A doctor put the new heart in a man. The man felt much better. He lived many more days.

This new heart became a big step. Many doctors learned from it.

Now, new hearts help many sick people. Some wait for a new real heart. Some use a pump each day.

New hearts give people more time. They help people live and hope.

versions.text:
An artificial heart is a man-made pump. It moves blood through the body. It helps a person stay alive when their own heart is too sick to work well. Some hearts become so weak they cannot pump blood on their own.

Long ago, doctors had no real plan for a very sick heart. It simply grew weaker over time. There was no proven way to fix such a problem.

In 1982, an inventor named Robert Jarvik built a new kind of heart. It was made of strong, man-made parts. It was not tissue from another person. He had spent years designing it.

A surgeon named William DeVries placed the new heart in a sick man. His name was Barney Clark. Clark lived many more days than doctors had thought he would.

This bold attempt became a major step for heart care. It happened more than forty years ago.

Artificial hearts now help many very sick people. Some wait for a donated heart. Others use a small pump to help their own heart along.

Artificial hearts give people more time. They let people hold onto real hope.

versions.title: A Pump for the Heart
versions.text:
An artificial heart is a man-made pump. It moves blood through the body. It helps a person stay alive when their own heart is too sick. A person does not need a donor heart right away to survive.

Long ago, doctors had no real plan for a heart that was failing badly. It simply grew weaker over time. There was no good way to fix it.

In 1982, an inventor in America built something new. Robert Jarvik had spent years building a man-made heart. It was made from strong plastic and metal parts. He wanted to give sick people more time to live.

A skilled surgeon named William DeVries placed the new heart in a very sick man. His name was Barney Clark. Clark lived many more days than most doctors had expected.

This bold attempt became a major step forward. Many later devices still follow ideas from it today, more than forty years later.

Artificial hearts now help many seriously sick people live longer lives. People use them to wait for a donor heart. Some people use them to recover after surgery.

Artificial hearts give people more time and real hope. They let a person keep living while doctors search for a longer fix.

versions.title: The Invention of the Artificial Heart
versions.text:
An artificial heart is a man-made pump. It moves blood through the body. It helps a person survive when their own heart can no longer work well. For some patients, it is simply the tool that keeps them alive.

Devices built to help a failing heart have existed for decades. Early versions were experimental. They rarely worked for very long. They were hard to fit inside the body.

That changed in 1982. An American inventor named Robert Jarvik had spent years designing a fully artificial heart. He knew the risks firsthand. Surgeon William DeVries, a skilled doctor, agreed to attempt something historic.

Working together, Jarvik and DeVries placed the new heart inside a dying patient named Barney Clark. It was built from strong plastic and metal, not human tissue. It kept Clark's blood moving for months.

That bold attempt became the model for later heart devices. Many still build on it today, more than forty years later.

Today, artificial hearts and heart pumps help many seriously ill patients survive. Doctors use them to keep a patient alive while waiting for a donor heart. Some use them as a longer-term fix.

Many modern heart pumps are small. They let patients walk, work, and travel. Other devices stay in hospitals, used only for a short time during recovery.

More than anything, an artificial heart means hope: more time to live and more time to heal.

Devices built to assist a failing heart have existed for decades. Early versions were highly experimental. They rarely worked for very long. They were hard to fit safely inside the body.

Everything changed in 1982. An American inventor named Robert Jarvik unveiled a strikingly different device. Jarvik had spent years designing a fully artificial heart. He understood the risks firsthand. Surgeon William DeVries, a determined doctor, agreed to attempt something historic.

Working closely together, Jarvik and DeVries placed the new heart inside a dying patient named Barney Clark. It was built from strong plastic and metal, not human tissue. It kept Clark's blood moving steadily for months afterward.

That bold attempt eventually became the model for later heart devices. Many still build on it today, more than forty years later.

Today, artificial hearts and heart pumps help many seriously ill patients survive longer. Doctors rely on them to keep a patient alive while awaiting a donor heart. Some use them as a longer-term solution entirely.

Many modern heart pumps are now small. They let patients walk, work, and travel freely. Other devices remain hospital-based, used only briefly during recovery.

More than anything else, an artificial heart represents real hope: the simple chance at more time to live and more time to heal.

versions.title: The Invention of the Artificial Heart
versions.text:
An artificial heart is a man-made pump engineered to move blood steadily through the body. It helps a person survive when their own heart can no longer function well enough on its own. For some patients, it is the critical tool that makes continued life possible at all.

Devices built to assist a failing heart have existed for decades, slowly evolving from simple external pumps. Early versions were highly experimental. They rarely worked for very long. They were difficult to fit safely inside the human body.

Everything changed in 1982. An American inventor named Robert Jarvik unveiled a strikingly different device. Jarvik had spent years designing a fully artificial heart. He understood the serious risks firsthand. Surgeon William DeVries, a determined specialist, agreed to attempt something historic.

Working closely together, Jarvik and DeVries implanted the new heart inside a dying patient named Barney Clark. It was built from durable plastic and metal, not human tissue. It kept Clark's blood circulating steadily for months, far longer than many had expected.

That bold attempt eventually became the blueprint for later heart devices. Many still build on it today, more than forty years later.

Today, artificial hearts and heart pumps help millions of seriously ill patients survive and recover. Doctors rely on them to sustain patients awaiting a donor heart. Some use them as a longer-term, independent solution.

Many modern heart pumps are now compact. They let patients walk, work, and travel with real freedom. Other devices remain hospital-based, used only briefly during recovery from surgery.

Whichever device a doctor chooses, the basic idea stays the same: an artificial heart should give a failing body enough time to heal, rather than leaving a patient with no option at all.

versions.title: The Invention of the Artificial Heart
versions.text:
An artificial heart is a man-made pump engineered to move blood steadily through the body when a person's own heart can no longer function well enough on its own. It is designed so a critically ill patient can gain enough time for recovery, a transplant, or simply a longer life.

Devices built to assist a failing heart have existed for decades across many hospitals, slowly evolving from simple external pumps into something far more sophisticated. Early records depict highly experimental, short-lived attempts. Those early devices, though, were difficult to fit safely inside the human body. They were nearly impossible to rely on for more than a few hours.

Robert Jarvik was born in Michigan in 1946. As a young engineer and medical researcher, he grew determined to solve one especially stubborn problem in medicine: a heart failing beyond repair, with no donor organ readily available.

Working for years in a research laboratory, Jarvik encountered earlier attempts at mechanical heart pumps, originally built mostly for animal experiments rather than genuine human use. He studied their underlying design, but no one had yet built a version reliable enough for a human patient to depend on.

Jarvik set out to refine the design significantly, improving its durability and its blood flow. He built a device from strong plastic and metal, powered by an external air-driven system, worn outside the patient's body. He completed his working design, called the Jarvik-7, by 1982.

That artificial heart became one of the first ever successfully implanted in a human being, when surgeon William DeVries placed it inside a dying patient named Barney Clark, who lived for 112 more days than doctors had expected.

Today, artificial hearts and heart pumps are used worldwide, across dozens of specialized hospitals, as both a bridge to transplant and sometimes a long-term solution on their own. Patients depend on them to survive, to recover, and to regain real independence.

Whichever device a doctor chooses, the basic idea stays the same: an artificial heart should give a failing body enough time to heal, rather than leaving a patient with no real option at all.

versions.title: The Invention of the Artificial Heart
versions.text:
An artificial heart is a man-made pump engineered to move blood steadily through the body when a person's own heart can no longer function well enough on its own, giving a critically ill patient time for recovery, a transplant, or simply a longer life.

Patients with severe heart failure once had essentially no reliable option beyond waiting, which made survival especially uncertain without an immediate donor organ.

Robert Jarvik was born in Michigan in 1946. As a young researcher interested in both engineering and medicine, he grew determined to solve one especially stubborn problem. Hearts were failing beyond repair, with no donor organ readily available at the right moment.

While working in a research laboratory, Jarvik studied various earlier mechanical heart pumps. These had been built mostly for animal experiments, not genuine long-term human use. He admired the underlying engineering, but no prior design had proven reliable enough for an actual human patient to depend on.

Jarvik set out to refine the design, over years of careful testing and revision. He built a device from durable plastic and titanium, powered by an external air-driven system worn just outside the patient's body. He completed his refined design, named the Jarvik-7, by 1982.

This innovative device eventually became one of the first artificial hearts successfully implanted in a human being. Surgeon William DeVries placed it inside a dying patient named Barney Clark. Clark survived 112 days longer than doctors had initially expected.

Today, artificial hearts and heart pumps are used worldwide, across dozens of specialized transplant centers, from temporary bridge devices to longer-term implants. Patients with severe heart failure depend on them daily to survive, to recover, and to regain genuine independence.

Many modern heart pumps now use small internal batteries rather than bulky external machines, letting a single compact device support a patient's circulation for months or even years without constant hospital supervision.

Artificial hearts ultimately gave patients with severe heart failure a dependable way to survive, heal, and live far more independently, long after Jarvik's own early designs had first begun.

MID.prompt: Using details from the article, explain what motivated Robert Jarvik to design the artificial heart, and describe its lasting impact on patients with heart failure.
checklist: Explains Jarvik's motivation for designing the device
Describes the key features of the artificial heart
Connects the device to its lasting impact on patients today
MID.modelAnswer: Robert Jarvik spent years designing a fully artificial heart because he wanted to give seriously ill patients more time to live, even without a donor heart available right away. In 1982, surgeon William DeVries placed Jarvik's device, built from plastic and metal instead of human tissue, inside a dying patient named Barney Clark, who survived 112 days longer than expected. That historic attempt became the blueprint most later heart devices build on, helping millions of seriously ill patients survive, recover, and regain their independence while they wait for a transplant.

HIGH.prompt: Analyze how the article uses evidence about both the limitations of earlier mechanical heart pumps and Jarvik's personal determination to explain why his invention became the enduring standard.

Explains how Jarvik's research background and determination shaped his invention
Connects his work to its lasting influence on patients with heart failure today
HIGH.modelAnswer: Before 1982, mechanical heart pumps remained experimental, largely tested on animals, and had not proven reliable enough for an actual human patient to depend on for more than a few hours. Robert Jarvik, a researcher trained in both engineering and medicine, grew determined to solve this stubborn problem: hearts failing beyond repair with no donor organ readily available. Devoting years to careful, painstaking testing, he built a device from durable plastic and titanium, the Jarvik-7, which surgeon William DeVries implanted in a dying patient, Barney Clark, who survived 112 days longer than expected. This historic success proved the design was reliable enough to build upon, and it ultimately became the blueprint that artificial hearts worldwide continue to follow, giving millions of patients with heart failure a dependable way to survive, recover, and await a transplant with genuine independence.
